title: S&P 500 Holds Steady Amid Yield Spike and Hopeful Strait of Hormuz Reopening【Live】
body:
Wall Street closed Thursday with the S&P 500 barely moving, caught between the upward pressure of soaring Treasury yields and the buoyant sentiment sparked by reports that the Strait of Hormuz may soon be fully reopened. While the broader market held steady, the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped for a third consecutive session, underscoring how higher‑interest‑rate expectations continue to weigh on the most rate‑sensitive sectors.

The bond market’s rally was the dominant theme of the day. The 10‑year Treasury yield nudged past 4.7 %, a level not seen since the early 2000s, as investors priced in the likelihood of another Federal Reserve rate hike later this year. Market participants cited persistent inflationary pressures in core services and a resilient labor market as the primary catalysts for the central bank’s hawkish stance. The yield surge has forced equity investors to reassess valuations, particularly for growth‑oriented stocks whose future cash flows are more vulnerable to higher discount rates.

In the equity arena, the S&P 500 finished essentially unchanged, hovering near the 5,400 mark. Technology and consumer discretionary names, which had been the primary drivers of the index’s recent gains, were largely flat, reflecting a cautious approach as investors weighed the cost of capital against earnings prospects. Meanwhile, the Dow’s decline was led by industrial titans such as Caterpillar and United Technologies, whose shares slipped amid concerns that higher borrowing costs could dampen capital‑intensive projects and slow the recovery of the manufacturing sector.

Geopolitical developments added a layer of optimism that helped temper the market’s nervousness about rates. The United Nations and several maritime security agencies signaled that the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint through which roughly a fifth of global oil shipments pass, is expected to be fully operational within weeks. The prospect of uninterrupted oil flow alleviates a key supply‑side risk that has kept energy prices elevated since the escalation of tensions in the Persian Gulf earlier this year. Crude futures responded positively, with Brent crude retreating modestly from its recent highs, suggesting that the market is already pricing in a smoother supply outlook.

Analysts note that the interplay between bond yields and geopolitical risk will likely dictate market direction in the near term. “We’re seeing a classic tug‑of‑war,” said Laura Chen, senior market strategist at Meridian Capital. “On one hand, the Fed’s tightening trajectory is pushing yields up, which is a headwind for equities, especially high‑growth names. On the other, the de‑escalation in the Gulf removes a major supply shock, supporting energy stocks and broader risk appetite.” Chen added that investors should monitor the Fed’s upcoming policy meeting for clues on whether the central bank will adopt a more aggressive stance or pause to assess the impact of recent rate hikes.

The mixed signals also raise questions about sector rotation. Energy and materials stocks have benefited from the easing of supply concerns, while consumer staples and utilities—traditionally defensive plays—remain attractive to investors seeking shelter from rate volatility. Meanwhile, the financial sector stands to gain from a steeper yield curve, as higher rates can improve net interest margins for banks and insurers.

Looking ahead, market participants will be watching several key data releases, including the upcoming consumer price index report and the Fed’s June meeting minutes, for further insight into inflation trends and monetary policy direction. If Treasury yields continue to climb, equity valuations could come under additional pressure, potentially reigniting a sell‑off in rate‑sensitive stocks. Conversely, a clear signal that the Strait of Hormuz is fully operational and that oil markets remain stable could sustain the modest optimism currently anchoring the market. In this delicate balancing act, the next few weeks will be crucial in determining whether the S&P 500 can break out of its sideways stance or succumb to the twin challenges of higher rates and lingering geopolitical uncertainty.
